name: Livedoid vasculopathy
aliases: PURPLE (painful purpuric ulcers with reticular pattern of the lower extremities)

reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / Fitzpatrick's Dermatology
clinicalPearls: A chronic thrombo-occlusive disorder of dermal vessels presenting with painful purpuric macules and recurrent ulcers of the lower legs, ankles, and feet
Healing leaves characteristic atrophie blanche: smooth, porcelain-white stellate scars ringed by telangiectasia and pigmentation
Pain is often disproportionate to the visible lesions and is a prominent, disabling feature
It is primarily a vasculopathy driven by intravascular thrombosis, not a true inflammatory vasculitis, so histology shows hyaline thrombi and fibrin with little primary vessel-wall inflammation
Frequently associated with thrombophilic and prothrombotic states, and screening for these is important
Disease is typically chronic with a seasonal (summer) flare pattern in many patients
Management is directed at reducing thrombosis and improving blood flow, using antithrombotic and other vasoactive approaches alongside wound care
reference.pathophysiology: Livedoid vasculopathy results from occlusion of dermal microvessels by fibrin thrombi rather than from primary inflammatory destruction of vessel walls. Hypercoagulable and prothrombotic tendencies promote intravascular thrombosis, causing localised ischaemia and infarction of the skin. The resulting tissue hypoxia produces the painful purpura and punched-out ulcers, and healing of these infarcts yields the sclerotic, avascular white scars of atrophie blanche surrounded by reactive telangiectasia. Because the process is occlusive, any inflammatory infiltrate is usually secondary, and identifying and treating underlying thrombophilia is central to control.
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy showing hyaline fibrin thrombi with minimal vessel-wall inflammation
Thrombophilia screen (including antiphospholipid antibodies and relevant clotting factor abnormalities)
Cryoglobulins and, where indicated, hepatitis serology
Assessment of venous insufficiency with duplex studies
Wound swab if secondary infection of ulcers is suspected
redFlags: Detection of an underlying thrombophilia or antiphospholipid syndrome requiring specialist management
Rapidly progressive or extensive ulceration with severe pain
Features suggesting an alternative systemic vasculitis or connective-tissue disease
reference.prognosis: Livedoid vasculopathy is a chronic, relapsing condition with recurrent painful ulceration and progressive atrophie blanche scarring; outcomes improve when an underlying prothrombotic state is identified and treated, though many patients experience persistent disease.
pitfalls: Mislabelling it as an inflammatory vasculitis and relying on immunosuppression rather than antithrombotic therapy
Failing to screen for thrombophilia and antiphospholipid syndrome
Confusing atrophie blanche scarring with simple venous stasis change
Underestimating the severity of pain and its impact on function
management: Give antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy (aspirin, dipyridamole, pentoxifylline or anticoagulation) to counter the fibrin-thrombus occlusion, the therapeutic mainstay
Screen for and treat any underlying thrombophilic or prothrombotic state
Provide effective analgesia for the disproportionate, disabling pain, including neuropathic agents
Deliver wound care and compression for lower-leg ulcers, treating secondary infection
Use intravenous immunoglobulin for refractory or severe disease
Advise smoking cessation and reduction of thrombotic risk factors
Arrange dermatology and haematology follow-up for the chronic, relapsing course
